lesson.title: On the Road: Solving Distance, Rate, and Time Problems
lesson.summary: Apply the distance equals rate times time formula, together with the applications of linear equations strategy, to find an unknown travel time for two objects moving apart.
lesson.body:
Distance, rate, and time problems all rest on one formula: distance equals rate times time, usually written d equals rt. Here rate means speed, such as miles per hour, distance means how far something travels, and time means how long the travel takes. Rearranging this formula algebraically, the same way you rearrange any equation to isolate a different variable, gives two useful alternate forms: rate equals distance divided by time, and time equals distance divided by rate. Which form of the formula to use depends on which quantity the problem asks you to find.

What makes these problems into applications of linear equations, rather than a single plug in step, is that most real distance rate time problems involve more than one moving object, or more than one leg of a trip, and the relationships between those pieces have to be translated into an equation before d equals rt can be applied. Two common setups appear again and again. In an opposite directions problem, two objects start at the same place and move apart, or start apart and move toward each other, and their speeds add together to give the rate at which the distance between them changes. In a same direction problem, one object chases another, and the difference between their speeds determines how quickly the gap between them closes.

Here is a worked example of the opposite directions type. Two trains leave the same station at the same time, traveling in opposite directions on straight tracks. One train travels at 60 miles per hour, and the other travels at 75 miles per hour. In how many hours will the trains be 405 miles apart? Since both trains travel for the same amount of time before the distance is measured, let t represent that time, in hours, for both trains. The first train travels a distance of 60t miles, and the second travels a distance of 75t miles. Because the trains are moving in opposite directions, the total distance between them is the sum of the two distances, so 60t plus 75t equals 405.

Combining the like terms 60t and 75t gives 135t equals 405. Dividing both sides by 135 gives t equals 3. The trains will be 405 miles apart after 3 hours. To check, find how far each train actually travels in 3 hours: the first train covers 60 times 3, which is 180 miles, and the second covers 75 times 3, which is 225 miles. Adding these two distances gives 180 plus 225, which equals 405 miles, matching the distance given in the problem exactly.

The same core equation, d equals rt, also underlies round trip problems, where a traveler covers the same distance going and returning at different speeds, and problems where a time difference rather than a distance is given. In every version, the strategy from applications of linear equations still applies: name the unknown with a variable, write an expression for each distance using d equals rt, translate the relationship between those distances or times into one equation, solve it, and check the result against the original description of the trip.
